Florida Building Code: Planning an Existing-Home Remodel

By Unique Building Contractors · October 23, 2026

The short answer

A remodel needs a scope-specific code review. Ask the design and construction team to confirm the applicable code edition and requirements for the existing building, proposed alterations and affected systems with the local building department.

Describe the work before asking what code applies

Replacing finishes, changing a floor plan and adding living space create different design questions. Explain the physical work instead of relying on labels such as cosmetic renovation. Include changes that may be hidden, such as a relocated drain, exhaust duct or electrical circuit.

Use the official DBPR code access page to locate Florida code resources. Have the responsible professional identify the provisions used for the permit package. An old drawing or a product brochure does not establish which requirements govern a new application.

Resolve existing conditions before final selections

Ask which measurements and observations can be completed before demolition. A proposed open kitchen may need a structural review; a new shower layout may need a drainage review. Do not assume a wall is nonbearing or a floor can accept a new opening from a photograph.

Create a decision log for conditions that cannot be verified until work is opened. Record the discovery, proposed response, cost implication and required approval. This makes changes easier to evaluate before they affect several trades.

Coordinate details across trades

For example, a kitchen hood affects cabinet dimensions, a wall or roof opening, electrical supply and the exhaust route. Ask one person to check that the drawings and installation instructions describe the same solution.

Keep approved substitutions in the project file. If an appliance or window changes after review, ask whether the revised selection changes the plans or permit requirements. Resolve that question before installation rather than at the final inspection.

Your planning checklist

  • Confirm the applicable code edition for the application.
  • List structural and trade changes.
  • Record unresolved existing conditions.
  • Review substitutions before installation.

Common questions

Does remodeling mean the entire house must be rebuilt to current code?

That is not a conclusion to draw from the word remodel. Applicable requirements depend on the work, existing conditions and the code review for that project.

Can a contractor promise code approval before reviewing the site?

A proposal can describe an intended approach, but approval depends on the actual documents, conditions and authority review.
